utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we go on and take a break afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we should give the numbers for those three documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D2586 will be MFI D795. 1D2585 will be Exhibit D796. And 1D2588 will be Exhibit D797.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, I just have two questions concerning an incident, the sniping of a tram on the 19th of June, 1994, which in this trial we call Incident F-8. I just want to clarify one point about the ballistics of that. Mr. Karadzic asked you, at page 14 of today's proceedings: "Were the fragments large enough in order to be able to establish the calibre?" To which you answered: "Well, ballistics experts can establish the calibre on the basis of those fragments. I mean, they were probably of sufficient size, since the calibre was established. "Q. Who was the ballistics expert in your team? "A. I really don't remember. I think it was Boro Stankov. I'm not sure." That's the end of the extract.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up P1758, and if we could go to page 7 in the English and page 10 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I just want you to look at the last paragraph of that, Mr. Vidovic. As you can see, it's a ballistics report relating to the incident on the 19th of June, 1994. And towards the end, we can see that the ballistics experts concluded that the fragments belonged to a 7.9-millimetre-calibre bullet, with tracing powder, and the bullets may have been fired from an M-48, 80-millimetre carbine -- 80-millimetre-calibre carbine rifle, automatic rifle, or an M-53 7.9-millimetre-calibre machine-gun. Do you see that in the final paragraph of this document?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is this what you were referring to when you said that calibre was established for this incident?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your testimony, Mr. Vidovic. Thank you again for your coming to the Tribunal to give it. Now you're free to go. I wish you have a safe trip back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break of 25 minutes. And I take it that the next witness is ready to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, he is ready. He's testifying under a pseudonym and with image distortion. He is ready to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So 25 minutes' break will be sufficient for preparation, I take it. We'll resume at five past 6.00. I meant five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we bring in the witness, can I hear from you, Mr. Tieger, what you're going to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. Let me make a preliminary point on that, and it will put the Court in a position to determine whether it wishes to hear the full submission today or later. And I'm certainly prepared to move to the full submission. The backdrop to this is the tendering, during the course of testimony, of an executive summary titled "The Truth About Gorazde" that was prepared by the Republican Research Committee. At that time, the Court MFI'd the document, asked for additional information from the Defence about that. The Defence submitted, on the 7th of October, some additional information, as requested by the Court. That was -- the submission in response to the Court's request was styled as a motion to admit the exhibit. I have no problem with that, but I have spoken with Mr. Robinson about it. We agreed that it, under the circumstances here, an oral submission -- oral response by the Prosecution would be appropriate, in light of the fact that it was raised in court would normally have triggered such a response. I wanted to make sure that at least that was our -- we are in a position to do that today, in case the submission of the written response was deemed as triggering some kind of dead-line, and wanted to make sure that was done. So that's the status. If the Court wants to hear it now, I can do so. If you want to find a more convenient time, that's perfectly acceptable with us, and with the Defence as well. I leave that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When do you think you can file it in writing, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the whole point was I think, Your Honour, this seems to me to be a situation where we can obviate the need to file it in writing, because it would trigger -- I've already explained to Mr. Robinson the substance of our proposed oral response. It just seems to me that we will move forward much faster, both -- and much more efficiently for the benefit of the Court, and obviating the need for additional burden on the parties, if I made this submission orally. It's just about a three- to five-minute submission. Maybe I shouldn't even have done the introduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are pressed by time, as always.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And given that we are not sitting for the remainder of this week, I wonder whether you can put it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As always, we're at the Court's disposal, of course, Your Honour. But as I say, if it helps, it's a relatively brief oral submission which has already been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. How brief would it be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly no more than five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much. I've already indicated what the backdrop is. I will note that at the time the Prosecution expressed some concern about the partisan nature of the document, in view of the fact that it was prepared by the Republican Committee, and factors associated with that. In fact, our brief -- we did some checking, as did Mr. Robinson, on the net to find something more about the document. That tended to underscore our concerns in that regard. We identified, for example, indications that a predecessor report by the same group and the same author triggered the resignation of four members of the committee, or from the other party, as I understand it, and also some indications on the net alleging an anti-Muslim bias by the author. But more important than that, and much more to the point here, I believe, Your Honour, is the fact that this is not the kind of document that has been the subject of our Bar Table discussions and has fallen within the ambit of proposed Bar Table submissions to date. We've been talking thus far about official, contemporaneous documents prepared by those involved in some manner actively in the conflict, whether they are the warring factions or perhaps international organisations gathering and assimilating information in order to deal with the situation on the ground. To the contrary, this is basically a kind of expert report which attempts to be or purports to be the assimilation of the kind of information we do bar table, and then an analysis and preparation of conclusions stemming from that assessment. Now, whether such an expert report is submitted to a committee of the US Congress, or to Harvard University, or to a think-tank, or to some particular interest group, doesn't change the nature of this kind of report, and the Court can well imagine how many such reports either party in this case might be interested in locating and tendering. And, indeed, if we were to do so, I think we'd be on the beginning of a very slippery slope, and we have something of an anomaly, submitting an expert report where -- that basically circumvents 94 bis, where the author isn't there to have his attitudes and methodology inquired about, and, indeed, where we don't know the sources. And in this particular case, the document is entirely unsourced. Now, one final point. And for full transparency, we have noted that this particular document was tendered by the Prosecution in one of the very -- in fact, in the first case in this Tribunal for a very limited purpose; for the jurisdictional purpose of international conflict and for one particular tiny point in the report. I wanted to mention that, in the interests of full transparency, but I don't think its tendering at a very early stage of the Tribunal's existence, before the development of procedures associated with expert reports, and for an extremely limited purpose, trumps the points I've made earlier. So for the reasons mentioned, should the Court -- certainly should the Court be inclined to admit this, we would argue its weight is extremely limited to non-existent. But more importantly, for the policy reasons I've just mentioned, we would suggest that this is not a report that is amenable to admission, at least under all the circumstances presented here. And I would also -- one final point. I think the relevant portion of the report, that is, the portion of the report the accused was interested in, was read out in full, and the accused obtained an answer from the witness, General Rose in that case, specifically to that portion. That might well obviate the need to even deal with the remainder of the report at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Would you like to respond -- to reply, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, very briefly. I think that since the report was discussed with General Rose, it would assist the Chamber, to understand the context of what was discussed and what is in the report, to have it as an exhibit, and to give it what weight that you believe is necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider the matter and issue the decision in due course. Before we begin to hear the evidence of the next witness, there are a couple of matters I'd like to deal with. First, there's an observation I would like to make in relation to the way in which you conduct the cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic. I noted that you introduced a lot of untranslated documents, and during the course of your cross-examination you just added the list of documents you were going to use during your cross-examination. At this moment, I just want to emphasise again that it is your responsibility to organise your team and your resources properly, and this should include organising the provision of notice of the documents you will be using on cross-examination, and making sure that those documents are all translated into English in advance. I hope you bear that in mind in the future. The next matter relates to the next witness. Mr. Karadzic filed a motion for modification of the protective measures that are currently in force for Witness KDZ166. These protective measures, which include pseudonym and image distortion, were granted by the Dragomir Milosevic Trial Chamber and, pursuant to Rule 75(F), continued to be in force in these proceedings. The Chamber notes that the accused requests the Chamber to address the issue of the witness's protective measures with him when he comes to testify. However, the Chamber sees no reason to revisit this issue again, given that the witness was consulted by the Prosecution this week and stated that he continues to have concerns about his safety. The Chamber notes that in the absence of the consent of the witness, a variation of protective measures can only be ordered in exceptional circumstances, as provided for in Rule 75(J) of the Rules. This witness has not agreed to any variation of his protective measures. The Chamber has considered the reasons provided by the witness, as set out in the Prosecution's investigator's report, and finds there are no exceptional circumstances which would justify a modification of the protective measures. Moreover, as required by Rule 75, the Chamber consulted with Judges Robinson, Mindua, and Harhoff, who composed the Bench in the Dragomir Milosevic case, who also agreed that there should be no modification of the protective measures in force. So, therefore, we deny the motion. That said, do we need to go into private session in order to bring in the witness? No. Let us bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Witness. Although it is a bit noisy, if you could kindly take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We didn't hear you because the microphone was turned off. Could you read it again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the Audio/Video unit could kindly show the witness his image, how he looks. Mr. Witness, do you see the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's how you will look to the other people, so the people in the public gallery and those who are watching these proceedings cannot see your face. And you will be referred to as "KDZ166" during the course of your evidence so the people outside will not know your real name. That's what you requested for. Do you understand? Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, and thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could I ask, first of all, for 65 ter 90197, please. This should not be broadcast. This is a confidential exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you confirm that you see on the screen in front of you your name? No need to read it out.

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes, I can see my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I request that that be admitted under seal, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1789, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've previously testified in the Dragomir Milosevic trial and in the Momcilo Perisic trial; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You have previously given several statements to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, I gave several statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've had an opportunity to review an amalgamated statement, which contains excerpts from your previous testimony and statements; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up Confidential Exhibit 22249, please. That's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you recognise that on the screen in front of you as an electronic copy of the amalgamated statement which you indicated you had an opportunity to review?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Does that statement accurately reflect your previous statements and testimony?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you were examined in court today on the same subjects, would you provide the same information to the Court in response to those questions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I request the admission of that under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I simply would like to point out that on page 15, there's an unscheduled incident on the 8th of November, 1994. Pursuant to our previous requests, we would ask that that be redacted from the statement, that there be no evidence concerning that incident elicited . And also there's one associated with exhibit 65 ter 16801, that we would ask to be excluded as connected with that incident. I'll say nothing more about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, do you have anything to add to what you stated earlier on?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I have no arguments different to those that I've already made on this subject, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber's ruling remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one further question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have you tendered the redacted public version of his amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I have not yet tendered a redacted public version. I can do so, and I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I propose to read a short summary of the witness's evidence for the benefit of the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to give a number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the under-seal statement will be Exhibit P1790, and the unredacted statement will be Exhibit P1791.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness was a criminal technician in Sarajevo during the conflict in Bosnia. His primary role was to attend crime scenes to take photographs, make formal sketches, and to collect parts of projectiles which had detonated there. The witness worked on over 100 cases of shelling or sniping of the civilian population of Sarajevo. His evidence focuses on seven of those cases: six shelling incidents and one sniping incident. Those incidents include: the killing of 8 and wounding of 18 persons in Dobrinja on 4th February 1994; the explosion of a modified air-bomb in Hrasnica on 7th April 1995, killing one person and wounding three; two shelling incidents on 24th May 1995, at Safeta Zajke Street, killing two and injuring five persons, and at Majdanska Street, killing two and injuring six; the explosion of a modified air-bomb on 16th June 1995, on Trg Medjunarodnog Prijateljstva, wounding seven persons; and a sniping incident in which Ms. Nermina Omerovic was killed on the 8th of November, 1994. That ends the summary, and, Your Honours, I'm going to start with Incident G-10.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you a few questions about the shelling in Hrasnica on the 7th of April, 1995. You remember your participation in that investigation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: To orient everyone, could I call up 13565, which can be in public. This is a map from the Sarajevo-specific court binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you see the green dot marked number 10. You've had an opportunity previously to review this map, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the green dot marked with the number 10 reflects the location of this incident?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask for an exhibit number for that, please, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1792.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, you say in your statement that you went to the scene of the shelling. That was on the same day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes, on the afternoon of the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Hrasnica on that day?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: We gathered together on that day at around 2.00 p.m. The whole team got together at the Public Security Station in Hrasnica. And after that, we went to the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: About how long did you spend at the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: We spent between two and three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you describe the general area in which the scene was located? Was it primarily commercial, industrial, military? Could you just describe the general nature?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the center of the Hrasnica neighbourhood, and there's nothing but family houses in this part. In the photographs that I made of that street, one can see only family houses and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I do not agree with you, Mr. Karadzic, that it was leading, as you said. Please go on, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could I ask for -- confidentially, can I ask for 09758, please. Now, if we could go to page 3 of this, please. If we could zoom in on that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Does this come from a dossier of photographs which you prepared?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you describe, in general terms, the nature of the destruction that you saw there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: This projectile landed in the yard where there was a larger house and a smaller house. Actually, it landed on the larger house and destroyed it completely; but not only that house. It destroyed the smaller house as well and another 11 houses in the general area within the radius of 100 to 200 metres. It blew away the roofs, it blew out the windows and the doors, and the doorjambs and window-panes, and it also blew away the roof tiles from all these houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can we -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Gaynor. Excuse me. Can we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it mean that you also tender the public version of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, we will prepare a public version of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I ask for page 15 of this document, please. Just the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe briefly your -- first of all, did you put the number markings on the ground, as photographed in this picture?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What does this particular photograph depict?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: This photograph was made in the interior of the house, and it shows the motor of the multi-barrel rocket-launcher, with a part of the cylinder with the rocket charge, and then the scale indicator is placed next to it so that you can see the size of the motor. 6 is marking some fragments of this air-bomb. And then this number 8 is the connecting sheet metal connecting the air-bomb to the rockets that were actually propelling it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Could I now ask for a sketch. It's 65 ter 09756. And could I ask that it not be broadcast. If we could go to pages 4 and 5 of the sketch, please. If we could also show the next page. I don't know if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the right of this screen in front of you, Witness, do you confirm that this is a sketch which you prepared which relates to this incident?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes, this is a sketch that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you've provided a legend with your sketch, so we won't go through every single item on it. But could you explain the dotted line that we see marked with the number 11? What does that represent?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: The dotted line represents the direction from which the projectile came.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The letter S above the dotted line indicates the direction north; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain, briefly, the information that you relied upon in drawing that dotted line?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: I drew the dotted line on the basis of information provided to me by one of the inspectors from the investigation team. I think his name was Hakija Hasan Efendic. He, in turn, got this information on the basis of a statement by an eye-witness who saw where the projectile was fired from. He saw it flying and dropping at this location in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could look at the previous page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Under item number 11, is it right that you've marked that the direction of fire was north-east? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the direction of the north-east, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask now for 65 ter 09757. Again, I'd ask that this not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you confirm that this is a report prepared by you relating to this incident in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Under paragraph 4, on the second line in the original, it says: "The projectile was fired from the south-west, where Ilidza is located." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain the inconsistency between this and the sketch that you created, which refers to the north-east as being the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: The north-west is referred to. The diagram refers to the direction of fire as being from the north-west. I made a mistake here, but I did mention the sector of Ilidza. That was just an error that was due to speed. I did say, after the comma, that the projectile came from the Ilidza area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I just clarify your answer there. Earlier on, you testified that the direction in your sketch was indicated as the north-east, and just now you've referred to the north-west. Your sketch - I can show it to you again - did say the north-east; isn't that right? Would you like to see your sketch again?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: I would, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask the Registrar, please, to bring back the sketch which is 09756.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see a dotted line on the sketch that indicates the direction from which the projectile came, and that is the north-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry, that's absolutely right. My mistake, Witness. Now, in your report, your report refers to the south-west. Now, my question was, just to clarify the position: Your report said the south-west and your sketch says the north-west. Which is correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: What is correct is what is on the sketch, and that is that the direction from where the projectile came was the north-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to the next incident, Your Honours, which is Incident G-11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It has been our practice to admit the documents when they are dealt with, so why don't we admit those three documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll give the numbers. But you're going to produce public versions in relation to all of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, if that's -- I can do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That may be consistent with the idea of public trials, so that we can have as many as possible in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. I would prefer that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we need to put them under seal, three of them all?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Those three should be under seal, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The proper numbers will be given now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter 09758 will be Exhibit P1793, under seal, and its public version will be Exhibit P1794. 65 ter 09756 will be Exhibit P1795, under seal, and its public version will be Exhibit P1796. And 65 ter 09757 will be Exhibit P1797, under seal, and its public version P1798.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to move now to the incident at Safeta Zajke Street on the 24th of May, 1995. Do you recall your participation in the investigation of that incident?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask for 65 ter 09773 to be brought up, please, and not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you see the first page of a photo documentation file, containing photographs which you took relating to this incident?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we have the third page, please. We can just show the B/C/S for the purposes of this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Before we look at the photographs, could you discuss -- could you describe generally what kind of area Safeta Zajke Street is? What is that -- what is the nature of that part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: This is the street which is -- it stretches in a straight line along the length of the north side of Sarajevo, and there are only family houses along that street; family houses, residential buildings. It's a residential area, mainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we focus in on the top photograph in front of you, could you describe, briefly, what we see here?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: This is a close-up of that location. You can see the place where the projectile fell. The projectile dropped directly onto the Safeta Zajke Street, on the asphalt surface. In the background, you can see the damage on the houses. You can see these tyres that are strewn about and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, there are other photographs in this file, which I won't show you, which show quite a lot of tyres. Can you explain what you know about those tyres?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: There is a car repair shop in that place, also a tyre repair shop. It's a place where cars are repaired, changes of tyres are done, so these are all activities related to car repair and maintenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we look at the photograph which is lower down on the same page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe what is depicted in this picture?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Number 1 marks the place where the projectile dropped, also the parts of the projectile. These are engines and the containers that contain the rocket fuel. Number 2 marks the crater in the asphalt, which was in the form of a funnel, in the form of an elongated cylinder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You placed the numbered markings at this location and took this photograph; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes, I placed the numbers and I made the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask for the seventh page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In photograph 11, which is on the top -- could we focus in on that, please. Could you describe what we see here?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: This is the place where the projectile dropped. An arrow indicates the direction from which the projectile came. This is an arrow that is marked in chalk on the asphalt. I made the photograph in the direction of the arrow. So the direction is that of the arrow, in the direction of this elongated funnel shape created by the projectile. In the background, you see the damaged house of Milica Vucicevic in the street of Safeta Zajke, number 41 [Realtime translation read in error "51"]. The house is still there today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: To make it easier to see, could you circle the line indicating the direction on --

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Safeta Zajke, it's wrong, it's wrong in the translation into English here. The number is 41, not 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you mark the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait until the usher comes to assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks] [Interpretation] This is the direction of the fire, and you can also see chalk marks, an arrow made of chalk, on the asphalt. You can see that. And then a little bit in front of that, you can clearly see the funnel shape created by the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In this specific instance, who determined the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: In this specific case, it was easy to establish the direction of fire because you could see the funnel. I did it, with the assistance of the people from the KDZ who were there. Durmo Salko was one of those people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that it wasn't your -- generally speaking, one of your duties to determine direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ166
utterances.text: Yes. My duty, in general, was not to establish the direction of the fire. This is something that is usually done by the people from the KDZ and by experts, forensic experts, ballistics experts. They are trained for this work. They are well-familiar with explosive devices, and they know what kind of effects they produce. And in cases like this, when a projectile drops, they always came with us to look at the area to see if any of the mine or explosive devices are left over. In this specific case, there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, that's sufficient. Could I ask that this photograph be admitted? It can be a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll be admitting this 65 ter 9773 under seal as Exhibit P1799, and 1800 for a -- is it a public version?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yeah, it can be public. There's no need to have an under-sealed version of this marked version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, not this marked --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The entire report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll admit this marked photo as Exhibit 1801. But if you, Mr. Witness, kindly put the date, which is 20th of October, and your signature on the bottom of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps not the signature, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Why don't you put your witness number, which is 166.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And today's date is 20th of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Time flies, Mr. Witness. I think that's it for today, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since we are not sitting for the remainder of this week and next Monday's holiday, the next sitting will be on Tuesday next week at 9.00. Mr. Witness, I apologise for your inconveniences, but I hope you would understand the difficulties the Chambers have in terms of scheduling. So during that break, you are not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 26th day of October, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
